title: Air India Warns of Flight Disruptions as UK Air Traffic Fault Grounds 2,000 Flights
excerpt: A technical failure at Britain's air traffic control provider NATS forced more than 1,750 flight cancellations on Tuesday, leaving over 330,000 passengers stranded. Air India advised travellers to check flight status before heading to the airport.
body:
• A technical fault at NATS, the UK's air traffic control provider, forced the cancellation of more than 1,750 flights on Tuesday, with another 291 scrapped on Wednesday.
  • Air India said it had been forced to "divert, delay or cancel multiple flights" to and from UK airports, warning that knock-on disruption could spread to its other services as aircraft and crew were left out of position.
  • The airline advised passengers to check their flight status before travelling to the airport, adding that it was closely monitoring the situation.
  • UK Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander met NATS chief executive Martin Rolfe and requested an investigation, while airlines including Ryanair and Wizz Air demanded sweeping reform of the system.

Air India has warned passengers to brace for further disruption after a technical failure at Britain's air traffic control provider forced the airline to divert, delay or cancel multiple flights to and from the United Kingdom earlier this week.

The fault struck the flight data processing system of National Air Traffic Services (NATS) on Tuesday, halting departures and arrivals across the country. NATS said the issue was resolved by 6:34 p.m. GMT and that "safety was not compromised," but warned that clearing the backlog would take time, according to Reuters.

Scale of the disruption

Aviation analytics firm Cirium counted more than 1,750 cancelled flights arriving into and departing from UK airports on Tuesday, while flight-tracking site Flightradar24 put the figure at over 1,300. A further 291 flights were cancelled on Wednesday, nearly all at Heathrow. Airlines UK, the industry trade body, said more than 330,000 passengers were affected.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=cuIBXqPvzeY

Heathrow suspended arrivals for the remainder of Tuesday while departures resumed, and the airport warned disruption would continue as airlines worked to reposition aircraft and crew. FlightAware data showed around 490 departures delayed across six airports — Heathrow, Gatwick, London City, Luton, Edinburgh and Bristol — with another 525 arrivals cancelled or delayed. British Airways was the hardest hit carrier at Heathrow, cancelling 16 of 333 scheduled departures, while Ryanair scrapped more than 50 flights on Tuesday and said 150,000 of its passengers had been affected by delays of up to eight hours.

Social media filled with images of passengers queuing with luggage through packed terminal halls. Josie Donoghue, stuck on a plane for three hours at Gatwick before her Ryanair flight to Ireland was cancelled, told the Associated Press: "Getting through that airport was like trying to get out of Alcatraz."

A failure the industry says keeps repeating

NATS apologised and said operations were "stable" by Wednesday, with a "full investigation" promised to identify any further action needed. But airlines reacted with fury at what they described as a recurring breakdown of critical national infrastructure.

Ryanair chief operating officer Neal McMahon called for NATS chief executive Martin Rolfe to resign, saying families, workers and visitors "have once again paid the price for NATS' abhorrent failure." Wizz Air declared the provider "simply not fit for purpose in its current form."

"A critical national infrastructure provider should not repeatedly bring the aviation system to a standstill. NATS is simply not fit for purpose in its current form."

— Wizz Air spokesperson

UK Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander met Rolfe on Wednesday, raising "significant concerns at the scale of disruption" and requesting an investigation, according to a Downing Street spokesperson. The Civil Aviation Authority said it would expect NATS to share a full report and would then consider whether further steps were needed to secure the reliability of the system.

The outrage has history behind it. In August 2023, a flight-plan processing failure at NATS cancelled hundreds of flights on the final day of the summer public holiday weekend. In 2024, a global IT software crash caused widespread delays at airports worldwide, including in Britain. Last year, a large fire near Heathrow forced the airport to shut down entirely, and a radar-related technical issue disrupted UK flights for more than four hours in July.

What passengers should do

Air India advised passengers to check the latest status of their flights before proceeding to the airport, warning that mispositioned aircraft and crews could delay even flights not originally affected by the UK outage.

"We regret the inconvenience caused by this unfortunate situation, which is entirely beyond our control, and thank our passengers for their patience and understanding."

— Air India, travel advisory on X

Heathrow, Gatwick and Stansted issued similar guidance on Wednesday, telling travellers to check with their airline before setting out. Qatar Airways also warned of delays and potential re-routing of flights to and from the UK. Passengers holding cancelled tickets are generally entitled to rebooking on the next available flight and, for long delays, meals and accommodation under UK passenger rights rules.

Diaspora angle

The UK-India corridor is one of the busiest long-haul routes in the world, and Air India's flights connect London Heathrow and Birmingham with Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru and other Indian cities. The timing lands awkwardly: September is a busy travel month for the diaspora, with students flying in for the academic term and families beginning to book ahead of the festive season.

For affected travellers, the practical advice remains the same: check your flight status on airindia.com or with your travel agent before heading to the airport, keep receipts for meals and hotels if you are stranded, and ask the airline about rebooking options before accepting a refund — taking a refund can cancel the airline's obligation to get you to your destination.

What's next

NATS says its investigation will determine exactly what failed in its flight data processing system — Rolfe told Sky News the company did not yet have "an idea yet of exactly what went wrong." The Civil Aviation Authority's review will decide whether NATS must overhaul its contingency plans, an area the regulator flagged as far back as 2024.

For airlines, the incident has revived a long-running argument about reforming Britain's air traffic control regime — a campaign that gained little traction after 2023 but now has the transport secretary's attention. For passengers on the UK-India route, the watchpoint is simpler: whether the backlogs clear fully in the coming days or bleed into further cancellations as crews and aircraft cycle back into place.
